paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Every hypothesis test can go wrong in two ways. A type I error, or false positive, rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true. A type II error, or false negative, fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false. Here a positive result means rejecting the null hypothesis, a negative result means not rejecting it, and false means the conclusion drawn is wrong.

paragraphs.heading: The courtroom picture
paragraphs.text: A hypothesis test works much like a trial. The null hypothesis plays the defendant: it is presumed true until the data give convincing evidence against it, just as a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty. The alternative hypothesis plays the case against the defendant. In this picture, a type I error is convicting an innocent person, and a type II error is letting a criminal go free.

paragraphs.heading: A medical example
paragraphs.text: Take the null hypothesis that a patient does not have a disease. Diagnosing the disease when it is absent is a type I error, and saying the patient is healthy when the disease is present is a type II error. Knowing about these two errors is put to wide use in medical science, biometrics and computer science.

paragraphs.heading: Putting numbers on the risk
paragraphs.text: The type I error rate is the chance that a test rejects the null hypothesis when that hypothesis is true. Tests are designed to keep that rate under a bound set in advance, the significance level, written with the Greek letter α. It is usually set at 0.05, meaning a 5% chance of wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis is accepted. The type II error rate is written β, and the power of the test equals 1−β.

paragraphs.heading: A trade-off you cannot escape
paragraphs.text: Statistical methods deal in probabilities, so we can never know for sure that a conclusion is right, and every test carries some chance of both errors. For a given sample set, pushing one error rate down generally pushes the other up. The risk can only be traded between the two, for example by moving the significance threshold. A stricter alpha, such as 0.01 instead of 0.05, is a simple and efficient way to cut type I errors.

paragraphs.heading: Where the two rates meet
paragraphs.text: The point where the type I and type II error rates are equal is called the crossover error rate, or CER. A system with a lower CER is more accurate than one with a higher CER. All else being equal, setting the two rates equal at the CER gives the lowest overall error rate.
